“Mrs. Boye—Mr. Lyhne. And Mr. Frithjof Petersen—Mrs. Boye.”

Erik made the introductions in Mikkelsen's studio, a bright, spacious room with a packed-clay floor and a ceiling twenty-five feet above it. Two large doorways at one end opened onto the yard; at the other, several doors led into smaller studios. Clay, plaster, and marble dust had turned everything grey. Overhead it thickened spiderweb threads until they resembled string; on the broad windowpanes it traced maps of rivers. It got into eyes, noses, and mouths. Along the shelves encircling the room, a jumble of casts displayed dust-outlined muscles, hair, and drapery, like a frieze depicting Jerusalem's destruction. Even the tall laurels in large tubs near one doorway were coated until they looked greyer than grey olive trees.

In the centre stood Erik at his modelling, a work blouse on his body and a paper cap over his dark, waving hair. A moustache had appeared, giving him a manly look beside the two friends who had just completed their bachelor's degrees. Still pale and worn from examinations, they looked properly provincial in clothes too new, with hair too closely clipped beneath rather oversized caps.

Not far from Erik's working platform, Mrs. Boye sat in a low chair with a tall back. One hand held an elaborately bound book, the other a piece of clay. She was small, very small, slightly brunette, with clear pale-brown eyes. Her skin glowed white, deepening in the shadows of her rounded cheek and neck to muted gold. This suited her glossy dark hair, which turned tawny blonde wherever the light struck it.

They arrived to find her laughing like a child: a long, joyful peal, merrily loud and wonderfully uninhibited. Her eyes too had a child's innocent directness. The open smile on her lips seemed younger still because a short upper lip left her mouth a little parted, revealing teeth white as milk.
Yet she was no child at all.

A little over thirty, perhaps? Neither the fullness beneath her chin nor her lower lip's ripe colour contradicted it. Her body was rounded, its firm, generous curves emphasized by a dark-blue dress, close-fitting as a riding-habit around waist, arms, and breast. A silk kerchief of muted crimson fell in ample folds round her shoulders and throat, its ends tucked inside her bodice's low, pointed neckline. Carnations of the same shade adorned her hair.
Glancing at the handsome book, Frithjof said, “I hope we haven't interrupted some enjoyable reading.”

“Not at all, not in the slightest. For the last hour we've been arguing over it,” Mrs. Boye answered. “When it comes to art, Mr. Refstrup is a thorough idealist. I find it all terribly tedious: crude reality must be purified, clarified, regenerated, and goodness knows what, until absolutely nothing remains. Just look at Mikkelsen's Bacchante, please—the one deaf Traffelini is carving in marble over there. Suppose I put her in a descriptive catalogue.... Good heavens! Number 77: A young lady in _negligé_ stands thoughtfully on both feet, wondering what to do with some grapes. I'd have her crush them—crush them until their red juice poured down her breast. Wouldn't that be better? Don't you agree?” In her eager, almost childish excitement, she caught Frithjof's sleeve and nearly shook him.
Frithjof conceded, “Yes, I do feel something is missing—a little freshness, perhaps—a certain spontaneity—”

“What's missing is simply naturalness. Good heavens, _why_ can't we be natural! Oh, I know the answer well enough: we haven't the courage. Artists and poets alike are too timid to acknowledge human nature as it actually is. But Shakespeare had the courage.”
From behind his model Erik observed, “You know, I've never really taken to Shakespeare. He rather overdoes things, I think. He spins you about until you've lost all sense of where you are.”

“I wouldn't go quite as far as that,” Frithjof objected, then added with a tolerant smile, “but equally I can't describe that great English poet's berserker frenzies as deliberate, intelligent artistic bravery.”

“Really? Goodness, how amusing you are!” She laughed heartily for so long that it tired her. Getting up, she wandered through the studio. Suddenly she turned towards Frithjof, opened her arms, and exclaimed, “God bless you!” Then she laughed again, almost folding herself in two.

Frithjof nearly took offence. But leaving in anger would be making too much fuss, particularly when he knew he was right; besides, the woman was very pretty. He remained and addressed Erik, carefully giving his voice an air of adult tolerance for Mrs. Boye to hear.
Mrs. Boye meanwhile drifted about the studio's far end, absently humming. At intervals the melody rose in a few swift, laughing trills, before falling back into slow and solemn recitative.
A bust of the young Augustus stood on a large packing-case. She started dusting it, then found clay and fashioned a moustache, a pointed beard, and finally earrings, attaching each to the head.

While she worked, Niels contrived to wander towards her, pretending to inspect the casts. She had not looked his way once, yet she must have noticed his presence. Without turning round, she extended a hand and asked him to fetch Erik's hat.
He placed the hat in her waiting hand, and she put it on Augustus's head.

Patting the disguised bust's cheek, she said, “Dear old Shakespeareson, foolish old man who never understood his own work! Was he just sitting there spilling ink when a Hamlet head appeared without his meaning it—was he?” She removed the hat and brushed his forehead with a motherly hand, as if smoothing back his hair. “Still, what a lucky fellow! More than half lucky, old poet boy!—You must at least admit he was a tolerable writer, this Shakespeare?”
A little irritated and blushing, Niels answered, “I admit to having an opinion of my own about the man.”
“Good gracious! Do you too have your own opinion of Shakespeare? Well, tell me what it is. Are you on our side or against us?” She posed beside the bust, smiling, an arm resting along its neck.

“I can't say whether this opinion, whose existence seems to surprise you, has the good fortune to gain importance by matching yours. But I believe I can call it _for_ you and your _protégé_. At least, I think he understood what he was doing, considered it carefully, and dared to do it. Often he dared despite doubt, and that doubt remains visible. Sometimes his courage went only halfway. Then he added details that blurred what he hadn't quite dared leave as he first conceived it.”
He continued speaking along these lines.

As he talked, Mrs. Boye became increasingly restless. Her eyes darted nervously first to one side and then the other, her fingers tapped impatiently, and a troubled expression clouded her face until it seemed positively painful.
Eventually she could restrain herself no longer.

“Please keep hold of your thought,” she burst out, “but Mr. Lyhne, I beg you to stop that hand movement, as if you were extracting teeth! Please, and don't let me put you off! There, now I'm listening perfectly, and I agree with you entirely.”
“Then there seems little point in my going on.”
“Why not?”
“If we're agreed?”
“If we're agreed!”

Neither intended anything particular by these final words. Yet they spoke as though delicate meanings filled them, exchanging subtle smiles like the fading gleam of a wit that had just passed between them. Each meanwhile wondered what the other meant, and felt faintly irritated at being too slow to grasp it.
They walked back to the far end of the studio, where Mrs. Boye settled again in her low chair.

Erik and Frithjof had talked themselves into a state of mutual boredom and welcomed their return. Frithjof came over to make himself pleasant to Mrs. Boye. Erik remained modestly in the background, as befitted their host.
Frithjof said, “If I were a curious person, I'd ask which book caused that argument with Refstrup just before we arrived.”
“Are you asking?”
“I am.”
“Ergo?”
Frithjof bowed in humble agreement. “Ergo!”

Holding the book aloft, she announced solemnly, “_Helge_—Oehlenschläger's _Helge_. Which canto? ‘The Mermaid visits King Helge.’ And which verse? The passage where Tangkjaer lies beside Helge, and he can no longer restrain his curiosity, so he turns
—_and at his side, With white arms soft and round, The greatest beauty he espied That e’er on earth was found._
_The maid had doffed her cloak of gray; Her lovely limbs were bare, Save for the robe like silver spray That veiled her form so fair._

That's the entire glimpse he grants us of the mermaid's beauty, and it's not enough for me. Here I want a rich, radiant picture, something so brilliant it leaves me breathless. I want to be admitted into the strange, mysterious beauty of a mermaid's body. What am I supposed to do with lovely limbs under a bit of gauze? Good heavens! She ought to be naked as a wave, surrounded by the sea's wild attraction. Her skin should carry something of a summer sea's phosphorescence, her hair something of the black, tangled terror of seaweed. Isn't that right? And a thousand watery colours should shift and glitter in her eyes. Her pale breast should have a sensual coolness; her limbs should flow like waves. Her kiss must hold the maelstrom's strength, and her embracing arms the yielding softness of foam.”
Her own words had set her glowing. Still alive with her subject, she stood regarding the young men with wide, questioning eyes like a child's.

No one said a word in answer. Niels had turned scarlet, and Erik looked intensely uncomfortable. Frithjof, entirely swept away, stared in frank admiration. Yet of the three he noticed least how captivatingly beautiful she was, standing within the enchantment her own words had made.

Within weeks, Niels and Frithjof called at Mrs. Boye's as regularly as Erik Refstrup. There, besides her pale niece, they encountered many young people: aspiring actors, poets, architects, and painters. They were artists more by reason of youth than ability, hopeful, brave, hungry for conflict, and quick to kindle with enthusiasm. A few were quiet dreamers, bleating yearningly towards yesterday's faded ideals. Most, however, overflowed with the ideas then considered modern. Modernity's theories intoxicated them, its energies drove them wild, its clear morning brilliance dazzled them. They were modern aggressively, modern extravagantly—perhaps especially because deep inside lay a strange instinctive yearning that had to be suppressed. The new spirit could not answer it, however universal, all-embracing, all-powerful, and all-illuminating that spirit claimed to be.

Even so, a storm's exhilaration filled their young souls. They believed in the light of thought's great stars, and their hope was deep as the ocean. Enthusiasm lifted them on eagle wings; their hearts swelled with the courage of thousands.

Life would doubtless wear this away in time, lull most of it to sleep. Worldly caution would destroy much, and cowardice would clear away whatever remained. But what did that matter? A time lived happily does not return in sorrow. Nothing the future brings can shrivel a day or erase an hour from the life already lived.

For Niels, the world was beginning to look different. Ten voices loudly announced the thoughts he had believed most secret and uncertain. His supposedly unique ideas had formed a mist-bound landscape, its outlines blurred, its depths unknown, its sounds subdued. Now that landscape stood uncovered in sharp, bright daylight, every detail plain, roads cut everywhere, people crowding along them. The very reality of what his imagination had created made it all seem strangely unreal.

He was no longer a solitary child-king ruling territories made by his dreams. He belonged to a crowd now, a man among troops, a soldier serving modern ideas. Someone had put a sword into his hand; ahead of him a banner flew.

What a marvellous, promising time! How strange to hear that vague, secret whisper of his soul ring through actual air: fierce, defiant trumpet calls, battering-rams thundering against temple walls, David's stone whistling at Goliath's forehead, triumphant fanfares. He seemed to hear himself speaking unfamiliar languages, with a clarity and force he did not possess, about what belonged to the deepest, most inward part of him.

The gospel of modernity, preaching dissolution and perfection, came from more than his contemporaries. Older men with respected names had also opened their eyes to the new ideas' splendour. Their language was grander, their conceptions more imposing. Names from earlier centuries followed in their wake. History stood beside them: world history, the history of human intelligence, thought's _Odyssey_. As young men they had felt the stirrings now exciting this generation and had testified to the spirit within. Then they had heard in their own voices that note which tells a speaker crying in the wilderness that he _is_ alone, and fallen silent. The young remembered only their speech, not their silence. They brought laurels and martyrs' crowns, eager to admire and happy in admiration. The honoured men did not reject this belated recognition. In good faith they accepted their crowns, saw themselves enlarged against history, and poetically removed the less heroic portions of their past. Their former convictions, cooled by hostile winds, soon glowed again as they talked.

Niels Lyhne's Copenhagen relatives, especially old Councillor Neergaard and his wife, thoroughly disliked his new circle. Modern ideas themselves were not the problem. Rather, some young men apparently considered long hair, enormous hunting-boots, and a little untidiness helpful to developing those ideas. Niels was no extremist in such matters, but seeing him with youths of that description was irritating, and having their friends encounter him so accompanied was worse. Yet all this counted for little beside his closeness to Mrs. Boye and his theatre outings with her and her pale niece.
Nothing definite could be alleged against Mrs. Boye, of course. But people talked. They had a great deal to say.

She came of good family, a Konneroy, one of the oldest and most distinguished patrician names in the city. Nevertheless, she had cut herself off from them. Some blamed the quarrel on a dissolute brother whom they had packed off to the colonies to be rid of him. The breach was certainly complete. There were even whispers that old Konneroy had cursed her and afterwards suffered a severe attack of his spring asthma.
This had all occurred after she was widowed.

Her husband, Mr. Boye, had been a pharmacist, an _assessor pharmacia_, and a knight. At his death he was sixty and possessed a barrel and a half of gold. As far as anyone knew, their marriage had been reasonably happy. During its first three years the older husband was deeply in love. Afterwards they pursued separate interests: he his garden and his reputation as an important man at gatherings of men, she the theatre, romantic music, and German poetry.
Then he died.

After a year's mourning, the widow travelled to Italy for two or three years, mostly spent in Rome. Stories that she smoked opium at the French club were untrue, as was the claim that she had posed for a sculpture like Paulina Borghese. The little Russian prince who killed himself while she was in Naples had not done so on her account. German artists did, however, serenade her endlessly. And one morning she really had dressed as an Albanian peasant girl and sat on church steps high in the Via Sistina. A newly arrived painter had hired her to pose, a pitcher on her head and a small brown boy beside her holding her hand. At any rate, a painting showing exactly that hung on her wall.

Returning from Italy, she met a fellow countryman, a celebrated and intelligent critic who would have preferred being a poet. People called him negative and sceptical, keen-minded, pitiless and harsh towards others because he treated himself just as harshly, believing this excused his brutality. Yet he was not quite the man they imagined. He was less repulsively unyielding, less sturdily consistent than he appeared. He constantly opposed the age's idealist tendencies and used disparaging names for them. Still, those dreamy, airy ideals attracted him: the intensely blue mysticism, the inaccessible heights, the lights that vanished as you watched. They appealed more strongly than the earthbound views he defended and, most of the time, believed.

Almost against his wishes, he fell in love with Mrs. Boye. He kept silent, for his love was neither youthful and open nor hopeful. To him she belonged to another race, finer and happier than his own. His love carried resentment, an instinctive fury against every sign of that finer breeding in her.

He examined her feelings, tastes, convictions, and outlook with jealous hostility. Every weapon he had—subtle eloquence, merciless reasoning, harsh authority, ridicule disguised as pity—was used to win her to his position. He succeeded. But once truth had triumphed and she resembled him, he discovered he had won too completely. He had loved her former self, her illusions and prejudices, her mistakes and dreams, not the person she had become. Disgusted with her, himself, and everything in his native country, he left and never returned. Just then, however, she had begun to love him.

Naturally this attachment supplied abundant material for gossip, and people made all they could of it. The Councillor's wife related the story to Niels in the tone elderly virtue adopts towards youthful transgression. His reaction both offended and appalled the old lady. He answered loftily about society's tyranny and personal freedom, the mob's vulgar respectability and the nobility of passion.
After that, he seldom visited his concerned relatives. Mrs. Boye, on the other hand, saw him more often than ever.
